bib.title: Selection-Inference: Exploiting Large Language Models for Interpretable Logical Reasoning

legacy_report:
SOURCE: Selection-Inference: Exploiting Large Language Models for Interpretable Logical Reasoning. Antonia Creswell, Murray Shanahan, Irina Higgins (DeepMind). **This file is arXiv v1 (2205.09712v1, dated 2022-5-20), a preprint. It is not the ICLR 2023 camera-ready.** If you cite it as ICLR 2023, check the numbers against the published version, because they may differ.

COVERAGE: I read all 82,732 of 82,732 chars across 33 pages: main text, references (skimmed), and appendices A–I (prompts, evaluation details, reasoning traces, limitations, baseline datasets, significance tests, Fig. S5 captions). Nothing was skipped. The figures themselves are images, so I could not read per-task bar values in Fig. 4b, Fig. 5 or Fig. S1. Only the numbers stated in the prose are reported below.

CLAIMS
- claim: The 7B model inside SI beats the same 7B model prompted directly (vanilla) and the same 7B model with CoT-style prompts, all scored generatively.
  number: 58.75% vs 2.94% (vanilla) vs 41.32% (CoT)
  setup: Gopher-family 7B, frozen, 5-shot prompts, no fine-tuning. Exact-string-match generative scoring, averaged over the selected logical tasks (bAbI 1, 2, 3, 15, 16; ProofWriter OWA depth 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, with Unknowns removed). SI runs a fixed number of steps.
  quote: "the 7B parameter LLM within the SI framework performs better (58.75%) than the same model evaluated naively (2.94%) or in the COT framework (41.32%)"
  where: p.8, Sec. 5
- claim: The 7B model with SI also beats the 40x larger 280B model, both vanilla and with CoT.
  number: 280B vanilla 31.19%, 280B CoT 44.03%
  setup: same as above, generative scoring
  quote: "also outperforms on average the 40x larger 280B parameter LLM in both vanilla (31.19%) and COT framework (44.03%)"
  where: p.8
- claim: The headline "over 100%" is SI-7B measured against the same-size vanilla 7B baseline on 10 tasks. It is not measured against CoT or 280B. The paper states the ratio three different ways, and none of them matches the Sec. 5 numbers (see PROBLEMS).
  number: "over 100%"; also "almost triples" vanilla and "almost doubles" CoT
  setup: 7B, 5-shot, no fine-tuning, 10 tasks
  quote: "yields a performance improvement of over 100% compared to an equivalent vanilla baseline on a suite of 10 logical reasoning tasks" / "it almost triples the performance of the same model used naively and almost doubles the performance of the same model used in the COT framework"
  where: p.1 abstract; p.3 contribution 3
- claim: On the easier multi-choice scoring, vanilla 7B beat vanilla 280B, and SI-7B, scored generatively, still beat both. The authors guess that the 280B model leans on stronger priors.
  number: 57.31% vs 51.45%
  setup: vanilla 5-shot, multi-choice scoring
  quote: "the vanilla 7B parameter LLM outperforms the 280B parameter LLM (57.31% vs 51.45%), while still performing signiﬁcantly worse than the 7B SI model"
  where: p.8
- claim: SI is the only model to fully solve bAbI 15 (deduction), with five examples in the prompt. It is significantly best on ProofWriter depth 0 and depth 1.
  number: 100%
  setup: 7B SI, 5-shot, bAbI run for 1 step
  quote: "the SI framework solves the bAbI 15 deduction task, the only model to achieve 100% accuracy"
  where: p.8
- claim: SI's advantage on ProofWriter shrinks as the number of reasoning steps grows. The authors put this down to a weak prompt-engineered Selection step.
  number: none
  setup: ProofWriter depth 0–5. A depth-d problem runs d steps (depth 0 runs 1 step), with at most two facts selected per step.
  quote: "with increasing depth, the gap between SI and the baselines diminishes. This is in part because prompt engineering is not suﬃcient to obtain an optimal Selection module."
  where: p.21, App. D.4
- claim: The trace is causal by construction. Selection may only copy facts from the context. Inference sees only the selection, not the question or earlier steps. So the answer cannot skip the reasoning. The authors contrast this with CoT, whose traces can be wrong while the answer is right.
  number: none
  setup: design property
  quote: "Each inference step is made in isolation, based solely on the limited information provided by the Selection module, without direct access to the question or to previous steps of reasoning."
  where: p.2
- claim: The CoT trace is not explicitly made causal, and CoT traces are often wrong even when the answer is right.
  number: none
  setup: citing Wei et al. 2022 supplementary
  quote: "the reasoning traces produced by the model are often wrong even when the ﬁnal answer is correct"
  where: p.3
- claim: Letting the model generate the selection freely led it to invent facts. Instead, selection scores each context fact by log-likelihood and picks the top one, repeating until the selection is complete.
  number: none
  setup: prompt-engineered Selection module
  quote: "this unconstrained approach may allow the model to make up facts, thus removing the causal aspect of the reasoning trace. Indeed during experimentation this is what we often found."
  where: p.7
- claim: Fine-tuning each module on single reasoning steps raises ProofWriter accuracy well above prompt-engineered SI and the baselines.
  number: 78.95% vs 57.93%; 7B vanilla/CoT 0.34/15.73%; 280B 31.58/21.12%
  setup: ProofWriter, 7B. Inference fine-tuned for 300 steps at batch 16. Selection fine-tuned for 4×10^4 steps at batch 16, taking 50 h on a TPU, and outputs sentence labels so it cannot invent facts.
  quote: "signiﬁcant improvements in ﬁnal reasoning accuracy (78.95%) over the prompt-engineered version of the SI framework (57.93%) and other prompt-engineered baselines (vanilla/COT generative 7B: 0.34/15.73%, 280B: 31.58/21.12%)"
  where: p.10, Sec. 6
- claim: Single-step entailment is easy. The fine-tuned Inference model passes 99% almost at once. Selection is the hard part because it requires planning, and it drops with depth to about 80%.
  number: >99% after 300 steps; ~80% selection accuracy
  setup: ProofWriter fine-tuning
  quote: "The Inference LLM converged very quickly to >99% test accuracy after only 300 ﬁne-tuning steps with a batch size of 16" / "the model still achieves high ( 80%) accuracy across most of the reasoning depths. Predicting early selections for deeper reasoning problems is hard, because it requires planning."
  where: p.10
- claim: Fine-tuned SI produces traces closer to the ground truth than a 7B model fine-tuned to emit every step in one pass, measured by Jaccard similarity. The one-pass baseline puts steps in the wrong order, adds steps that are not needed, and repeats steps. Values are in Fig. 5b only.
  number: none
  setup: ProofWriter, 7B
  quote: "while the baseline model is good at predicting most of the reasoning steps, they often appear in the wrong order, there are additional reasoning steps that are not on the minimal reasoning path, and some steps get repeated a number of times."
  where: p.10
- claim: Vanilla LLMs handle single-step entailment well but weaken with distractors, with facts they must recall themselves, and with more steps. Even the 280B model is barely above chance on logic tasks.
  number: 13.6% above chance; 38 multi-choice logic tasks; 50 tasks total
  setup: Gopher family, 5-shot
  quote: "even the largest 280B model performed only 13.6% above chance level on average across the 38 available multi-choice logic tasks"
  where: p.5
- claim: Irrelevant context hurts. On 2WikiMultiHop, adding Wikipedia paragraphs lowered accuracy, and giving only the relevant structured facts more than doubled it.
  number: 13.62% → 1.47% → 1.97% → 35.55% (decimal points restored, see PROBLEMS)
  setup: Gopher family, exact match, dev subset
  quote: "the models scored1362 343% on average on the original dataset ... the performance dropped to147 1202%on average ... resulting in197 139% accuracy ... resulting in 3555 4787% average accuracy."
  where: p.31, App. H
- claim: More SI iterations can recover from errors and raise accuracy, mostly at depth 1. Because there is no halting rule, the paper reports results at a fixed step count.
  number: none (Fig. S1)
  setup: ProofWriter
  quote: "Fig. S1 shows how the number of SI steps can lead to improved performance. There is greater improvement to performance for depth-1 reasoning."
  where: p.21–22

LIMITS
- The authors call it a "proof of concept". There is no halting: it runs a fixed number of steps and takes the final inference as the answer.
- Selection is the main point of failure, and they cannot quantify this because there are no intermediate labels for the prompt-engineered tasks.
- It assumes that the given context holds every fact needed and that every question is well posed and answerable. It needs a retrieval step for real-world use.
- Unknown answers were dropped from ProofWriter. bAbI 1–3 and 15 were run for one SI step, so "multi-step" is tested mainly on ProofWriter and bAbI 16.
- Tasks were hand-picked (10 of 50). The baselines are one model family (Gopher, closed), and the CoT baseline is only "COT inspired".
- No verifier is used, so a false inference can be added to the context. The authors list verifiers, trace search and handling ambiguous questions as future work.
- Dated: the models are Gopher 7B and 280B with 2022-era few-shot prompting. There is no comparison to self-consistency or later CoT variants.

BUILDS ON: Wei et al., 2022 (chain of thought, the baseline); Tafjord et al., 2020 (ProofWriter, which also generates one step at a time, and the closest prior work); Rae et al., 2021 (Gopher, scaling); Andreas et al., 2016 (neural module networks); Mao et al., 2019; Yi et al., 2018; Hudson and Manning, 2019; Garcez and Lamb, 2020 (neurosymbolic); Nye et al., 2021a (scratchpads); Cobbe et al., 2021; Zelikman et al., 2022; Min et al., 2022 (choice of 5 shots); Weston et al., 2015 (bAbI).

CODE
- Selection prompt template, p.6: `<fact>. We know that <fact>[ and <fact>]*. Therefore,`
- Inference prompt, p.7: `# Problem to solve.` / `<output of the Selection module>. Therefore,`
- Algorithm 1 loop, p.7: "whilenot halt() do / 𝑠𝑡 Selection_Module„𝑝𝑠𝑒𝑙𝑒𝑐𝑡𝐶 𝑡𝑞 LLM” / 𝑖𝑡 Inference_Module„𝑝𝑖𝑛𝑓𝑒𝑟 𝑠𝑡” / 𝐶𝑡‚1 𝐶𝑡[𝑖𝑡". In plain terms: select from context and question, infer from the selection only, then append the inference to the context.
- Stop-selection trick, p.21: "we append". Therefore, " as a choice to the context that the model can select."
- bAbI 2 SI example, p.17–18: "Reason: at t=1 daniel got the apple there. We know that at t=4 daniel went to the bedroom. Therefore, the apple is in the bedroom."

FIGURES
- Fig. 1, p.2: vanilla vs CoT vs SI prompt structures side by side. The clearest single picture of "split one call into alternating constrained calls" (fits 06-chaining) and of how SI differs from CoT (fits 03).
- Fig. 2, p.3: qualitative bAbI traces, including recovery from an error and an ambiguous answer. Shows faithfulness and inspectability concretely.
- Fig. 4, p.9: (a) average accuracy for 7B/280B × vanilla/CoT/SI, (b) per task. This is the headline result chart. Its caption says "11 datasets" but the text says 10.
- Fig. 5, p.11: (a) Selection accuracy by depth after fine-tuning, (b) Jaccard trace accuracy, SI vs all-at-once.
- Fig. 3, p.5: logic scales worse than other BigBench tasks, and accuracy drops with step count.
- Fig. S1, p.21: accuracy vs number of SI iterations.

PROBLEMS
- The captions command in scripts/papers/figures.py printed nothing, because these captions read "Figure 1j" with a stray "j" glyph. I found the pages by searching the text instead.
- Decimal points, "<" and "±" were dropped in extraction. "𝑝 001" is probably p<0.01. "𝑝 = 0012" and "𝑝 = 0034" are probably 0.012 and 0.034. "1362 343%" is probably 13.62 ± 34.3%. I quoted these verbatim; the restored values are my reading of them.
- Internal inconsistencies. The abstract's "over 100%" vs vanilla, "almost triples" vanilla, and "almost doubles" CoT do not match 58.75 vs 2.94 (about 20x) or vs 41.32 (about 1.4x). Fig. 4a's caption says 11 datasets while the text says 10. Sec. 6 gives prompt-engineered SI as 57.93% and vanilla 7B as 0.34%, apparently ProofWriter-only, against 58.75% and 2.94% in Sec. 5. Pick one figure and give its setup. Do not cite "100%" on its own.
- The paper's ICLR identity is not shown by this file (v1 preprint).
- No embedded instructions found.
